1.pericope_label: Putting the unclean out of the camp

schools.summary: Gill dates the command after the camps were formed and the people numbered, against Jarchi, who assigns it to the day the tabernacle was raised, and observes that Miriam was afterwards put out by this law; he passes on Aben Ezra's conjecture that the defiled travelled between the standards of Ephraim and Dan, marking that the text does not say it. Calvin denies that the expulsion was medicine at all. God was not acting as a physician consulting the people's health; by joining to the lepers those with an issue and those defiled by the dead he was exercising them in the pursuit of purity, teaching them to keep away from all uncleanness. The reason given confirms it, all the habitations of his elect people being parts of his sanctuary, which it was a shame to pollute; and Calvin turns on the licence men give themselves in mixing sacred things with profane, the worst of them boasting to be no less zealous than others and sparing not to lift up polluted hands.

Henry makes the timing the point: the camp had just been modelled and set in order, and to complete the reformation it must next be cleansed, for the purity of the church must be as carefully consulted as its peace, the wisdom from above being first pure and then peaceable. The tabernacle was now fixed in their midst, and the greater profession any family makes the more it is bound to put iniquity far from its tent. He reads the expulsion as a figure with two references. It shows what the governors of the church ought to do, separating between the precious and the vile and purging out scandalous persons as old leaven, for it is for the glory of Christ and the edification of his church that the openly and incorrigibly profane be kept from communion until they repent. And it shows what God himself will do in the great day, purging his floor and gathering out of his kingdom all things that offend, as here the unclean were shut out and into the new Jerusalem no unclean thing shall enter.

Clarke supplies the practical arrangement, each camp having ground behind and to one side where the infected might be lodged, since we cannot suppose they were driven into the naked wilderness; this is the earliest account of such separations, and probably gave the first idea of a hospital. He allows three reasons for it — the diseases were contagious, the camp was God's habitation, and it was an emblem of the Church — then presses a pastoral point against both parties in a familiar dispute. Sinners must be separated, but treated with affectionate regard, because they may be reclaimed; too often a backslider is abandoned by all, and the man who might have been recovered by tender treatment grows incurably hardened. To hold that he cannot finally fall makes him secure, and to hold that he must perish makes him desperate, and either way leaves him inactive about his own soul; in a state of probation, Clarke answers, any man may fall through sin and any sinner may be renewed to repentance. Wesley hears a warning that men may be made guilty by other men's sins, and a duty of avoiding converse with the wicked.

Keil sets the chapter in its place: having organised the tribes outwardly as the army of Jehovah, the law now turns to their inward moral and religious order, so that their unity should have support from within. Since the Holy One dwelt in the midst of the camp, those defiled by leprosy, by an issue, or by touching a corpse were put outside it, male and female alike.

schools.summary: Calvin narrows the offence: though it seems at first to include all trespasses, the precept concerns only things stolen or fraudulently withheld, and secret thefts at that, which are not usually brought to justice, so that a man may not plead ordinary custom or the number of his companions for excuse. Without restitution the confession would be illusory, since fraud contracts a contamination never purged until the house is cleared of the gain; and the added fifth is meant less to enrich the loser than to make all beware of an offence that costs the doer, the want of one's property for so long being often the greater injury. On the missing kinsman he thinks recompense to the priest very uncommon, most dead men leaving some successor, but necessary, since otherwise the grossest offender would never hesitate to plunder an heirless estate. He gives three grounds for assigning the holy things to the priests: lest what is dedicated be profaned by promiscuous use, lest the rich come emulously to gain applause and put the rest up for sale, and because the ministers of the altar should live by the altar. Gill notes why the law is repeated at all, Jarchi finding two novelties in it: that no fifth part and no trespass offering fall due on the testimony of witnesses until the man confesses, and that what is taken by violence from a proselyte goes to the priests; he also reports Fagius's form of the confession, in which the man owned himself worthy of stoning or strangling or burning.

Clarke states the rule flatly: without confession there is no hope of mercy, and without restitution God will not forgive, for how can a man with his neighbour's property in hand expect mercy from a just and holy God? On the heirless case he grants that a stranger in the camp might have no relative in any tribe. Wesley takes sins that men commit for sins against men, and holds that the words against the Lord are added to show that injuries done to men are also sins against God, who has commanded justice to men as well as religion to himself; the guilt in view, he says, is the man's being sensible of it, convicted in his own conscience. He adds that the fifth is at once compensation for the long want of the goods and a penalty to discourage others, and explains why the priest receives what is left over: he was God's deputy to take his dues, that he might the more cheerfully devote himself to holy things. On the hallowed things he draws a line of his own — these cannot be the sacrifices, since part of those was offered to God and the remainder eaten by the offerer as well as the priest, but such other things as were devoted to God and could not be offered at all, a man consecrating a house, for instance, and the house becoming the priest's.

Keil states the principle first: no crime against a neighbour's property was to remain without expiation in a congregation encamped around the sanctuary, because such crimes involved unfaithfulness towards Jehovah himself.

not the sacrifices at all, since the offerer ate part of those, but things devoted which could not be offered — a consecrated house, for instance

11.pericope_label: The law of jealousy and the offering

schools.summary: Calvin moved this ceremony out of its place among the legal services because it belongs to the seventh commandment. Its object is that women should not abandon themselves to unchastity on a hope of escaping punishment, and that jealousy should not breed dissension; by it God proclaims himself the avenger of wedlock. He then meets an objection: to speak of a wife who goes aside while the offence stays concealed looks absurd, since if the fact were established the test would be useless; but the condition refers to the husband's opinion, so that a man who thinks his wife unfaithful may appeal to God for a judgment beyond the reach of man. He adds that the crime seems named on purpose, lest husbands heedlessly involve innocent wives in disgrace, since many are causelessly suspicious, and once jealousy has taken possession there is no room for moderation; to grant such a power to a cruel husband would be like putting a sword into the hands of a madman. Of the offering he marks how far the rite stands from the others, being an ordeal in which the woman exposes herself to a curse, so that pure meal is used, expiation not according with it. Gill sets out the Misnah's procedure, the husband proving before his local court that he had warned her and then being sent to the great sanhedrim at Jerusalem, where the judges tried to terrify her as in capital cases before using smooth words, and describes the husband's state of mind as a thought rising in the mind, a suspicion he cannot throw off.

Henry states the sin before the remedy. Adultery is going aside from God and virtue; it is a trespass against the husband, robbing him of his honour, bringing a spurious breed into his family and breaking his covenant. It is besides a sin the parties take care to conceal, so that the eye of the adulterer waits for the twilight; it would not covet secrecy were it not shameful, and the devil who draws men to it teaches them to hide it. Against that concealment stands the husband's suspicion, which Solomon calls the rage of a man, cruel as the grave. He draws two admonitions: wives should abstain from all appearance of uncleanness, since a little fire may kindle a great matter; and husbands should entertain no causeless suspicion. He gives the judges' persuasion in the woman's own hearing — dear daughter, perhaps thou wast overtaken by wine, or carried away by the heat of youth — and notes that one who confessed was not put to death but divorced and lost her dowry. The offering he calls coarse, barley meal without oil or frankincense, suited to an afflicted household, for a great affliction it is either to have cause for jealousy or to be jealous without cause; it is an offering of memorial because the action appeals to the omniscience and justice of God.

Clarke pauses on the phrase for the husband's state of mind, which may mean a diabolic influence or simply the passion of jealousy. Wesley reads the statute as given partly to deter wives from adultery and partly to secure them against the rage of hard-hearted husbands, who on mere suspicion might destroy them or put them away; a wife's jealousy carried no like danger, she having neither authority nor opportunity. He gives two reasons for the missing oil and incense: it was a kind of sin offering, from which both were excluded, and she came as a delinquent, wanting the grace oil signified and the acceptance frankincense meant; the offering brought iniquity to remembrance before God and in her conscience, and a woman innocent of this charge would recall others.
Keil explains why an ordeal was needed: the crime was denied, no witness could support it, and she had not been taken in the act, so no other way remained.

outliers.claim: warns that the statute could be abused — to give this power without distinction to a cruel or ungodly husband would be like putting a sword into the hands of a madman

the spirit of jealousy come upon him

16.pericope_label: The bitter water and the oath

schools.summary: Gill cites the two Targums with Jarchi and Aben Ezra for taking the holy water out of the laver, and adds from Jarchi that a woman who owned herself defiled tore the writing of her dowry and went out; Ben Gersom sets the rest facing the holy of holies.

Clarke calls the water holy because consecrated to sacred uses, and notes that this is the most ancient case on record of trial by ordeal; he reports the Jewish supposition that the earthen vessel had never been used, and thinks the dust meant to mark the baseness of the crime charged. On the uncovering of the head he reads a public humiliation, since to take off a woman's veil and expose her to men's sight would be counted a great degradation in the East, and Paul appears to allude to the practice. He explains that being made a curse and an oath means her name and punishment would be cited as a terror to others, as Jeremiah names Zedekiah and Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire for villany in Israel; and he is less confident about the symptoms, which cannot easily be ascertained, though since thigh and feet are used delicately in Hebrew for what nature conceals, the falling of the thigh probably means a prolapse following the abdomen's preternatural distension. He hears an allusion to the passage in Paul's warning that whoever eats unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself, and observes that this is the first place where amen appears as a concluding wish in prayer, its root meaning to be steady and permanent. Wesley asks what the holiness of the water was for, and answers that a guilty woman might fear to add profaneness to her crime; the vessel was broken afterwards so the memory of the business might be blotted out, and the dust is an emblem of vileness taken from the tabernacle floor to strike the greater terror. On the uncovered head he looks inward and upward, partly that she might be made sensible how manifest all her ways were to God, partly as a token of sorrow. He says the offering was placed in her hands that she might offer it herself and call God to witness her innocency, and glosses the water's name twice: bitter from the taste the dust gave it or from its effects, and causing the curse not by natural power but by a supernatural efficacy.

Keil takes the water from the basin before the sanctuary, and marks what the oath assumes before it threatens: it is called an oath of cursing, yet it first supposes the woman innocent and assures her the water will then do no harm, and only afterwards does the priest turn the charge into imprecation. When the Amen is said, the priest writes the curses in a book-roll and washes them off in the water, so that the words themselves pass into it — a symbolical act setting forth that God gives the water its power.

23.pericope_label: The trial, its effects, and the law summed up

schools.summary: Gill says the words of the curse were written at length in a scroll, and, some report, her name with them, but not her double amen; of the drinking he gives the rule in its harshest form, that once the roll was blotted out she must drink whether she would or not, and only confession stopped it, the water being poured away and her offering scattered. He accounts for two small cruelties as calculated pressure: the offering she held throughout was heavy, an omer of barley flour in a basket of palm twigs, put into her hands to weary her, that with her mind distressed she might the sooner confess; and if after the blotting she refused the cup they compelled her. On the handful burnt he reports Aben Ezra's neat turn, that it was a memorial for good if she was innocent and for evil if not. He defends the law's running only one way, since the greater authority of the husband would seem lessened if the wife had such a power, a family suffers more by a wife's adultery, and women in those times were more prone both to suspicion and to the sin itself. He adds a hard note on the innocent woman, who, having by unbecoming behaviour raised the suspicion and refused to be reclaimed, justly bore the infamy — one Maimonides says innocent women would have given all they had to escape.

Clarke explains how words could be washed into water at all: the curses were written with an ink prepared without any calx of iron to make a permanent dye, so that they came off the parchment into the cup and the woman drank the very words of the execration, the ink used in the East being nearly all of this kind, so that a wet sponge will efface the finest writing. He declines the rabbinic guess that a bitter substance was mixed in, since Moses intimates nothing of the kind, and takes the word for affliction and death, which Scripture also calls bitter. Of the acquitted woman he reports the tradition with warmth: she had great honour and became strong, healthy and fruitful, bearing sons where she had borne daughters and finding easy travail where it had been hard. He ends by ranking the statute the most singular law in the whole Pentateuch, and one almost every nation of the earth appears to have copied, similar trials being used wherever evidence was wanting and men looked for their god to interfere for justice. Wesley reads the blotting as itself a sign, the curses coming to nothing if she were innocent, and takes the promise of seed to mean she would certainly bear children, the Jews holding she did so infallibly even if barren before; on the closing verse he agrees with Gill that the husband would not have been guiltless had he connived at a loose way of living without reproving her, nor if he had nursed his jealousy in secret and gone on to hate her.

Keil states the acquittal briefly, that a woman not defiled remains free, and denies that the law's partiality is real: it was framed for the woman only because a man might marry more than one, but in the statute of Leviticus the man stands level with the woman in the matter of adultery, so the appearance of unfairness is removed. He observes why nothing is said of a wife refusing the oath — refusal would amount to confession, and she would be put to death as an adulteress, and not she alone but the adulterer with her.
